item.title: DR Congo Threatens Exit Over Francophonie Leadership Dispute
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Original headline: Macron urges unity as Francophonie summit opens in Cambodia
The Francophonie summit opened in Phnom Penh as French President Emmanuel Macron sought to prevent DR Congo from withdrawing over leadership disputes. The Organisation internationale de la Francophonie (OIF) faces a critical vote to elect its next secretary-general, with Rwanda’s Louise Mushikiwabo seeking a third term. DR Congo, home to 57.3 million French speakers, threatened to leave if Mushikiwabo is re-elected, accusing Rwanda of supporting the M23 armed group in eastern Congo. Rwanda denies the claims and insists Mushikiwabo remains in the race. DR Congo withdrew its candidate, Juliana Lumumba, and endorsed former Romanian PM Dacian Ciolos, conditional on Rwanda stepping aside. Macron warned against internal divisions, urging unity, but Rwanda rejected French pressure. France, the OIF’s largest donor, faces criticism for its influence. UN Special Rapporteur Tom Andrews called on Cambodia to release detained activists, stressing no one should be imprisoned for human rights advocacy.

item.title: James Gleick links telephone history to modern tech evolution
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Technology Original headline: Hello? James Gleick's new book compares the history of the telephone to the modern era
James Gleick's book 'The Telephone: A New History' explores the evolution of telephone technology and its parallels to modern digital communication. Gleick discusses how early phone etiquette, like the use of 'hello,' emerged organically among users rather than being dictated by inventors. He notes that Alexander Graham Bell and his assistant Tom Watson initially used terms like 'ahoy' for phone calls but soon adopted 'hello' by the early 1870s. The telephone spread rapidly in the U.S., with most urban areas adopting home phones by 1880. Gleick argues the telephone revolutionized society by accelerating communication and reshaping time perception, similar to today's internet and AI. He highlights the telephone's role in fostering connection and warns of historical patterns of monopolies and corporate control, drawing parallels to modern tech giants. Gleick emphasizes that users should reclaim control over technology, echoing the grassroots development of phone etiquette. The book traces how the telephone's invisible influence shaped modern life, from social norms to economic systems.

item.title: Wall Street Rising Stars of the Last Decade Highlighted
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: From Goldman Sachs to Citadel, see 10 years of Wall Street rising stars who made their mark
Business Insider's Rising Stars of Wall Street series, launched in 2017, profiles young professionals who have risen to leadership roles at firms like Goldman Sachs, Blackstone, and Citadel. Over the past decade, the series has highlighted individuals who have reshaped finance through innovation and strategic moves. Many honorees have since taken on executive positions, influencing industry trends. The latest 2026 class includes top investors, traders, and dealmakers, with insights into their educational backgrounds and career trajectories. The series also tracks the current roles of past honorees, showcasing their ongoing impact in a competitive industry. Topics include networking strategies, AI-era skills, and career transitions beyond traditional finance.

item.title: Nvidia's Madison Huang rises as potential successor amid leadership transition
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: Jensen Huang's daughter was on the rise inside Nvidia. Succession may have come too soon.
Madison Huang, daughter of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, has risen to a senior role at the company as it seeks a new leader. As senior director of product marketing for physical AI, she has gained influence beyond her title, with former employees noting her assertiveness and strategic impact. However, her lack of technical expertise raises questions about her readiness to replace her father, who exited Nvidia amid personal scandals and a board investigation. Huang's background in business and marketing, rather than engineering, has positioned her as a potential successor but not yet a viable replacement. She has taken on key roles in Nvidia's partnerships, including collaborations with Foxconn and LG, and has influenced internal operations by coordinating cross-functional teams. Despite her growing influence, she faces challenges from veteran executives and must balance her role as a leader without technical deep expertise. Huang's career path, which included a stint as a chef and hospitality marketer, contrasts with her current position, though she has demonstrated resilience in learning Nvidia's technical jargon. Her visibility extends beyond the company, including meetings with tech leaders in South Korea and advocacy for smaller AI firms. Nvidia's leadership transition remains uncertain as it navigates reorganization and succession planning.

item.title: Italy Imposes Record Fine on Meta for Privacy Violations
item.description:
Source: BBC News, ABC News: Top Stories, Deutsche Welle
Italian regulators fined Meta €805 million for accessing Android users' photos and videos without explicit consent, the largest penalty ever imposed by Italy on a tech company. The Data Protection Authority ruled Meta violated a European privacy directive requiring 'free and informed consent' for data access. The fine, 0.47% of Meta's global turnover, targets a Facebook app feature that suggested phone gallery photos as post ideas without clear disclosure. The DPA found the feature, activated by default, allowed Meta to access private data without notification, affecting 20 million Italian Android users. Meta has 60 days to disable the feature and seek separate consent. The DPA cited Meta's 'lack of cooperation' during the investigation. A Meta spokesperson called the fine 'disproportionate' and stated the feature 'helps people post photos with user permission,' planning to appeal. The DPA rejected Meta's claim the case should fall under Irish jurisdiction, noting data pertains to Italian users. The fine follows a separate US court ruling ordering Meta to pay $25 billion for misleading users about data practices. The DPA emphasized the 'high number of people affected' and ongoing violations for some users.
item.source: BBC News, ABC News: Top Stories, Deutsche Welle

item.title: New Mexico's Free Childcare Program Faces Capacity and Funding Challenges
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: News Original headline: New Mexico wanted free childcare for all. This is what's worked — and what hasn't
New Mexico launched a universal free childcare program in 2025, making it the first state to offer childcare to all eligible families. The program, funded by the Land Grant Permanent Fund, has enrolled about 50% of children under 5, but demand far exceeds capacity. Families face long waitlists, with some waiting over a year for spots. Providers like Kids Campus and Mrs. Olga's Daycare report high demand and limited slots, leaving many children without access. Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham called the program transformative but acknowledged the need for expansion. The state plans to create 12,000 new childcare spots, though it’s only halfway there. A copayment of up to $148.50 per month will apply to wealthier families earning over $198,000 annually. Critics, like Republican Sen. Steve Lanier, argue universal childcare strains budgets and should target lower-income families instead. Meanwhile, rural areas struggle with childcare deserts, and providers face workforce shortages. Despite challenges, New Mexico’s experiment is drawing national attention as a model for expanding early childhood access.

item.title: Surfliner train kills two pedestrians near Ventura County beach
item.description:
Source: LA Times Original headline: Surfliner 'train versus pedestrian' accident kills two: It happens 'more than people think'
Two people were struck and killed by a northbound Pacific Surfliner train near Faria Beach Park in Ventura County on Friday night. Officials have not determined why they were on the tracks. Ventura County Fire Department Capt. Tony McHale said the train was stopped at the scene, with no injuries to passengers. McHale noted such incidents occur more frequently than public awareness suggests, citing cases involving suicide, homeless individuals, or accidental trespassing. California has the nation’s highest railroad trespassing and grade-crossing fatalities. From 2021 to 2025, 20 people died along the Surfliner route, 19 due to trespassing and one at a grade crossing, according to California Operation Lifesaver. The 351-mile Surfliner route serves San Diego, Los Angeles, and San Luis Obispo, carrying 2 million riders annually.

item.title: 11 Silicon Valley founders ousted from companies they founded
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: 11 Silicon Valley tech founders who were cast out from the companies they helped build
Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO after an extramarital affair scandal and board investigation. Founders being ousted from their companies is common, with examples including Steve Jobs, Elon Musk, and Sam Altman. Jobs left Apple in 1985 over management clashes, later returning as CEO. Altman was ousted from OpenAI in 2023 but reinstated days later. Jerry Yang of Yahoo resisted Microsoft's $44 billion buyout offer, leading to his resignation. Jack Dorsey was fired twice from Twitter, first in 2008 and again in 2020. Sam Bankman-Fried's FTX collapsed in 2022, leading to his 25-year prison sentence. Elon Musk was ousted from PayPal in 2000. Martin Eberhard sued Tesla after being pushed out in 2007. Travis Kalanick resigned from Uber in 2017 amid scandals. Eduardo Saverin's Facebook stake was diluted, leading to a lawsuit settled in 2009. Andrew Mason was fired from Groupon in 2013 after a stock plunge. Palmer Luckey left Meta in 2016 after donating to a pro-Trump group, though Zuckerberg denied political bias. Luckey stated he donated $9,000 to a Trump-supporting group.

item.title: Nigeria Warns Against High-Altitude Travel Through Ethiopian Airport
item.description:
Source: BBC News Original headline: Nigeria cautions against travel via Ethiopia's main airport due to altitude
Nigeria's government has warned citizens, especially those with medical conditions, against traveling through Ethiopia's Bole International Airport due to its high altitude. The foreign ministry in Abuja cited 16 Nigerian deaths this year linked to the airport, which sits at 2,334m (7,657ft) above sea level. Officials urged individuals with cardiovascular or respiratory issues to seek medical guidance before traveling through Addis Ababa, emphasizing the risks of high-altitude environments. Experts note that thin air reduces oxygen intake, straining the heart and lungs, which can lead to heart failure in those with preexisting conditions. The ministry stressed it does not intend to deter travel but wants to ensure safety. The airport serves as a major transit hub for Africa, the Middle East, and Asia, handling millions of passengers annually. The warning highlights the dangers of altitude for vulnerable populations, including dizziness, fatigue, and breathing difficulties, which can worsen for people with lung diseases.

item.title: UPS cargo plane collides with Copa Airlines jet on Miami taxiway
item.description:
Source: ABC News: Top Stories Original headline: UPS plane, Copa Airlines flight collide on taxiway at Miami International Airport
A UPS cargo plane and a Copa Airlines passenger jet collided on a taxiway at Miami International Airport on Saturday night. The incident occurred around 9:15 p.m. when the wingtip of a Copa Boeing 737 struck the nose of a UPS Boeing 767. Two people were treated for minor injuries at the scene but did not require hospitalization. Air traffic controllers instructed the UPS crew to yield to the Copa flight, according to the FAA. The FAA is investigating the collision, which caused visible damage to the UPS aircraft. Airport operations were unaffected as flights were rerouted. UPS stated its crew is safe and committed to cooperating with authorities. Copa Airlines did not immediately comment. A pilot on the UPS flight was heard saying, 'Somebody hit us' on air traffic controller audio. The airport confirmed no disruptions to flight schedules.

item.title: Tomb of the Unknown Soldier's Guards Honor Duty and History
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic Original headline: What the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier Means to Its Guards
In 1921, Edward Younger, a World War I veteran, was chosen to select the Unknown Soldier from four identical caskets. Overwhelmed, he placed roses on a casket and delivered it to Arlington National Cemetery. The tomb, completed in 1932, became a solemn site for remembrance. Guards, part of the 3rd Infantry Regiment, perform 24-hour duty, maintaining strict protocols. In 2023, Specialist Thomas Iglesias reprimanded Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for disrupting the tomb’s silence, earning a commendation. Guards, like Younger, reflect on duty and loss, with many having served in multiple conflicts. The Vietnam Unknown was identified in 1998, ending future unknown burials. Younger, who later died at Arlington, saw the Unknown Soldier as a symbol of every unnamed soldier. The tomb remains a place where guards and visitors honor those whose names are lost to history.

item.title: AI Handles 90% of Code at CIQ, Yet Struggles to Hire Engineers
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: AI writes 90% of the code at this company. It still can't hire enough engineers.
CIQ, a company that manages complex computing systems, now relies on AI to write over 90% of its code, according to president Bjorn Hovland. Despite this automation, the company struggles to hire enough experienced engineers. Hovland noted that demand for senior developers has surged, with the firm hiring almost no junior developers. AI generates vast amounts of code, but human oversight is critical, especially for systems used by major corporations and governments. CIQ founder Gregory Kurtzer demonstrated AI's capabilities by creating a Linux-compatible operating system kernel in 11 days. He warned that programmers resistant to AI risk falling behind, as experienced engineers using the technology can achieve greater productivity. The shift highlights a growing need for deep technical understanding over manual coding. However, the traditional path to becoming a senior developer is becoming harder as companies bypass junior roles. Hovland advised young developers to build personal projects and learn system fundamentals to prepare for the evolving landscape.

item.title: Asia Society's Lizzi C. Lee on big tech restrictions after Nvidia espionage claims
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: Technology
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after allegations of an improper relationship with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based executive linked to a data center company, Megaspeed. Megaspeed, which grew from a Chinese gaming firm, acquired over $4.6 billion in Nvidia hardware in two years, expanding rapidly. Lizzi C. Lee of the Asia Society notes concerns about Megaspeed's potential ties to Chinese interests, including ownership transfers through offshore entities and its role in providing computing power to Chinese companies via Southeast Asian data centers. She highlights legal distinctions between direct chip shipments to China and remote access via overseas facilities. Investigators are examining whether Megaspeed received preferential treatment from Nvidia and whether restricted chips were illicitly transferred. Beijing denies any involvement, and no evidence has been publicly proven. The case raises questions about U.S. tech export controls and China's access to advanced AI hardware.

item.title: Veteran raises funds for rare cancer research after diagnosis
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Original headline: Marine Corps veteran diagnosed with rare skin cancer rallies CSUSM fraternity to fund disease research
Marine Corps veteran Jason Beyer, 45, was diagnosed with porocarcinoma, a rare skin cancer typically affecting older adults. Despite VA coverage, Beyer reached out to his Kappa Sigma fraternity at Cal State University San Marcos to raise funds for rare disease research. The fraternity is organizing a fundraiser ending Nov. 15 to support the National Organization for Rare Disorders. Beyer noted the cancer's unusual location on his foot and age of onset. Fellow brother Jake Peeler praised Beyer's impact on military peers. Beyer now volunteers with CSUSM's Special Collections, interviewing veterans and asking them to leave messages for future generations. He credits his work with fellow veterans for keeping him grounded during treatment. Beyer expressed gratitude for community support, stating it helps him and his family.

item.title: Werner Holzer Prize Winners Highlight Journalism's Role in Democracy
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Original headline: Werner Holzer Prize awarded to Katja Gloger and DW's Jaafar Abdul Karim
The Werner Holzer Prize, honoring foreign journalism, was awarded to Katja Gloger and Jaafar Abdul Karim. Gloger, a veteran Russia correspondent, received first prize for her critical reporting on German-Russia relations and her book exposing policy misjudgments. Abdul Karim, a DW journalist, won second prize for his talk show JaafarTalk, which fosters dialogue across the Arab world and Germany. The award ceremony in Frankfurt highlighted press freedom challenges. Gloger emphasized the need for fact-based journalism, citing Reporters Without Borders data showing only 1% of people access independent media. She dedicated the prize to journalists in exile and Novaya Gazeta. Abdul Karim stressed journalism's role in bridging divides, urging open dialogue against hate speech and polarization. The jury praised his programs for promoting cross-cultural understanding. A research grant also went to Luise Land, exploring German colonial legacy in Namibia. Both winners called for resilient, inclusive journalism amid rising threats to press freedom.

item.title: AI Could Add 2 Million Jobs Globally by 2030, Study Says
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Original headline: What job apocalypse? AI could add almost 2 million new jobs on net by 2030.
Gartner projects AI will create 10.6 million new global jobs between 2025 and 2030, offsetting 8.9 million job losses, for a net gain of 1.7 million. John Lovelock, Gartner analyst, explained companies initially delay hiring due to AI uncertainty, then reduce roles as adoption grows, eventually adding jobs. Over 435 million workers may need to adapt to AI changes, with tasks shifting significantly. Nicole Bachaud noted AI is reshaping tech roles and skills demanded, increasing industry volatility. Challenger, Gray & Christmas reported over 100,000 AI-related job cuts in the U.S. this year. Workers like Cristina Estupiñán and Shawn Mrzena expressed skepticism or disinterest in AI-driven changes. Goldman Sachs’ Jan Hatzius warned of temporary labor market pressures from AI adoption but predicted low unemployment. Lovelock highlighted sector differences, with governments likely to cut jobs for efficiency while service industries may see growth. Pew Research found 76% of Australians and South Koreans expect AI to reduce jobs, with younger workers more concerned than older adults.
